<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" viewBox="0 0 1280 720" width="1280" height="720">
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="topBarGrad" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#F6821F"/>
      <stop offset="60%" stop-color="#1A6FC4"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#0D1B2E"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>

  <!-- Background -->
  <rect width="1280" height="720" fill="#0D1B2E"/>

  <!-- Top gradient bar -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="6" fill="url(#topBarGrad)"/>

  <!-- Header area -->
  <rect x="0" y="6" width="1280" height="74" fill="#0A1628"/>
  <rect x="0" y="6" width="4" height="74" fill="#EF4444"/>

  <!-- Slide title -->
  <text x="40" y="54" font-family="'Arial Black', Impact, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">6.5% of Traffic Mitigated: Persistent Threats and Bot Concentration</text>
  <text x="1240" y="54" text-anchor="end" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#64748B">06</text>

  <!-- Takeaway box -->
  <rect x="40" y="88" width="1200" height="44" rx="4" fill="#2D1515"/>
  <rect x="40" y="88" width="4" height="44" fill="#EF4444"/>
  <text x="56" y="115" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">6.5% traffic mitigation and Log4j's persistence 3+ years post-disclosure confirm that the threat surface is broad, constant, and slow to close.</text>

  <!-- TOP ROW — 3 KPI Cards -->

  <!-- KPI 1 — 6.5% mitigated -->
  <rect x="40" y="150" width="375" height="130" rx="8" fill="#2D1515"/>
  <rect x="40" y="150" width="375" height="5" rx="3" fill="#EF4444"/>
  <use data-icon="shield" x="56" y="170" width="28" height="28" fill="#EF4444"/>
  <text x="100" y="186" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#EF4444" letter-spacing="1">TRAFFIC MITIGATED</text>
  <text x="213" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="'Arial Black', Impact, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="58" font-weight="bold" fill="#EF4444">6.5%</text>
  <text x="213" y="272" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">of all Cloudflare-processed traffic</text>

  <!-- KPI 2 — 68% bot traffic -->
  <rect x="433" y="150" width="374" height="130" rx="8" fill="#1A2A1A"/>
  <rect x="433" y="150" width="374" height="5" rx="3" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <use data-icon="bug" x="449" y="170" width="28" height="28" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <text x="493" y="186" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#F6821F" letter-spacing="1">BOT TRAFFIC CONCENTRATION</text>
  <text x="620" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="'Arial Black', Impact, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="58" font-weight="bold" fill="#F6821F">68%</text>
  <text x="620" y="272" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">from just top 10 countries</text>

  <!-- KPI 3 — RPKI +6.4% -->
  <rect x="825" y="150" width="415" height="130" rx="8" fill="#0F2A1F"/>
  <rect x="825" y="150" width="415" height="5" rx="3" fill="#22C55E"/>
  <use data-icon="shield-check" x="841" y="170" width="28" height="28" fill="#22C55E"/>
  <text x="885" y="186" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#22C55E" letter-spacing="1">ROUTING SECURITY (RPKI)</text>
  <text x="1033" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-family="'Arial Black', Impact, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="58" font-weight="bold" fill="#22C55E">+6.4%</text>
  <text x="1033" y="272" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">RPKI valid routes increase in 2024</text>

  <!-- BOTTOM LEFT — Threat Landscape -->
  <rect x="40" y="298" width="590" height="360" rx="8" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="40" y="298" width="5" height="360" fill="#EF4444"/>

  <text x="60" y="326" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">Threat Landscape</text>
  <rect x="60" y="332" width="554" height="1" fill="#2D4A6A"/>

  <!-- Most attacked sector -->
  <rect x="60" y="344" width="554" height="60" rx="6" fill="#2D1515"/>
  <use data-icon="target" x="76" y="358" width="22" height="22" fill="#EF4444"/>
  <text x="110" y="364" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#EF4444">Most Attacked Sector</text>
  <text x="110" y="385" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">Gambling & Games</text>
  <text x="110" y="400" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Highest attack volume industry category observed</text>

  <!-- Log4j persistence -->
  <rect x="60" y="416" width="554" height="80" rx="6" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="60" y="416" width="4" height="80" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <use data-icon="triangle-exclamation" x="76" y="430" width="22" height="22" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <text x="110" y="434" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#F6821F">Log4j Still Actively Exploited</text>
  <text x="110" y="454" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">CVE-2021-44228 — disclosed December 2021</text>
  <text x="110" y="472" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Continues to be targeted 3+ years after initial disclosure</text>
  <text x="110" y="490" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B" font-style="italic">Underscores persistent nature of widely known vulnerabilities</text>

  <!-- Bot stats -->
  <rect x="60" y="508" width="554" height="64" rx="6" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="60" y="508" width="4" height="64" fill="#64748B"/>
  <use data-icon="globe" x="76" y="522" width="22" height="22" fill="#94A3B8"/>
  <text x="110" y="526" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">Bot Traffic Geographic Concentration</text>
  <text x="110" y="546" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">68% of global bot traffic from top 10 countries</text>
  <text x="110" y="564" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Highly concentrated origin geography for automated attacks</text>

  <!-- Strategic note -->
  <rect x="60" y="584" width="554" height="56" rx="4" fill="#112240"/>
  <text x="76" y="604" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#38BDF8">Strategic Implication:</text>
  <text x="76" y="622" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Continuous patching, zero-trust architecture, and</text>
  <text x="76" y="636" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">behavioral threat intelligence are non-negotiable in 2025</text>

  <!-- BOTTOM RIGHT — Email Security -->
  <rect x="650" y="298" width="590" height="360" rx="8" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="650" y="298" width="5" height="360" fill="#F6821F"/>

  <text x="670" y="326" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">Email Security Threats</text>
  <rect x="670" y="332" width="554" height="1" fill="#2D4A6A"/>

  <!-- Email KPI -->
  <rect x="670" y="344" width="554" height="90" rx="6" fill="#2D1A0D"/>
  <use data-icon="envelope" x="686" y="360" width="26" height="26" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <text x="1030" y="375" text-anchor="middle" font-family="'Arial Black', Impact, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="52" font-weight="bold" fill="#F6821F">4.3%</text>
  <text x="840" y="378" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">of emails processed</text>
  <text x="840" y="400" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">were <tspan fill="#EF4444">malicious</tspan></text>
  <text x="840" y="420" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Identified via Cloudflare email security analysis</text>

  <!-- Deceptive link metric -->
  <rect x="670" y="448" width="554" height="60" rx="6" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="670" y="448" width="4" height="60" fill="#EF4444"/>
  <text x="704" y="468" font-family="'Arial Black', Arial, sans-serif" font-size="26" font-weight="bold" fill="#EF4444">43%</text>
  <text x="760" y="466" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">contained a deceptive link</text>
  <text x="760" y="484" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Designed to trick recipients — most common malicious payload</text>
  <text x="760" y="500" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#64748B">Of all malicious emails processed</text>

  <!-- Top malicious TLD -->
  <rect x="670" y="520" width="554" height="56" rx="6" fill="#1A2E47"/>
  <rect x="670" y="520" width="4" height="56" fill="#F6821F"/>
  <text x="704" y="542" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="15" font-weight="bold" fill="#E8F0FE">Top Malicious TLD:
  <tspan font-size="20" fill="#F6821F"> .bar</tspan></text>
  <text x="704" y="562" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Largest share of malicious and spam email origin domain</text>
  <text x="704" y="574" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="12" fill="#64748B">Monitor unconventional TLDs in email filtering policies</text>

  <!-- Email strategic note -->
  <rect x="670" y="588" width="554" height="52" rx="4" fill="#112240"/>
  <text x="686" y="608" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#38BDF8">Strategic Implication:</text>
  <text x="686" y="626" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="13" fill="#94A3B8">Advanced email security with link analysis and TLD-based</text>

# 01_cover

Welcome to the Cloudflare Radar 2024 Year in Review. This annual report synthesizes data from Cloudflare's global network — one of the world's largest — covering Internet traffic, technology adoption, connectivity disruptions, and security threats observed throughout 2024.

The three headline numbers on this slide frame the scope: a 17% traffic growth rate, 225 major disruptions, and 6.5% of all traffic requiring mitigation. [Pause] These are not outliers — they are the new baseline.

[Scan Room] This briefing focuses on what these numbers mean for your infrastructure and security strategy in 2025.

Key points: (1) 2024 data sourced from Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver and global network (2) Report covers traffic, services, technology, disruptions, and security (3) Data represents the state of the global Internet
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_traffic_growth

[Transition] Let's begin with the macro picture: how much did the Internet grow in 2024, and who is driving that growth?

Global Internet traffic grew 17% year-over-year. [Data] That is nearly one-fifth more traffic than 2023 — driven by commerce, communications, entertainment, and an expanding user base. [Pause]

The headline surprise is Starlink. [Data] SpaceX Starlink traffic grew 3.3 times — meaning the satellite network delivered more than triple the traffic volume versus the prior year. [Benchmark] This growth rate dwarfs the global 17% average by nearly 20x, reflecting genuine infrastructure buildout into previously unserved regions.

[Scan Room] The 41% mobile share and 28% IPv6 adoption complement this picture — connectivity is diversifying in both medium and protocol.

Key points: (1) 17% YoY traffic growth continues multi-year upward trend (2) Starlink 3.3× signals satellite as serious infrastructure tier (3) Mobile and IPv6 adoption reflect infrastructure diversification
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_top10_services

[Transition] With more traffic on the network, the question becomes: where is that traffic going? The top 10 services ranking tells us.

Google held the #1 position for the second consecutive year, followed by Facebook, Apple, TikTok, and AWS. [Pause] The top five represent search, social, hardware, short-form video, and cloud infrastructure — a snapshot of where digital attention concentrates.

The most strategically significant trend, however, is not in the table. [Data] Generative AI services continued their rapid ascent throughout 2024, while Metaverse-associated services retreated. [Benchmark] The shift from Metaverse to Generative AI represents a complete inversion of enterprise technology investment narratives from just two years ago.

[Scan Room] For network planning purposes, the continued dominance of Google, Meta properties, and AWS means your peering and caching strategies for these platforms remain highest-priority.

Key points: (1) Google #1 for 2nd year, stable top-5 composition (2) Generative AI fastest-rising category — strategic investment signal (3) Metaverse decline confirms AI as dominant enterprise tech vector
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_tech_adoption

[Transition] Beyond where traffic goes, we also saw dramatic shifts in *how* it travels and *how* it is protected.

The most significant story is post-quantum encryption. [Data] At the start of 2024, approximately 2% of TLS 1.3 traffic used post-quantum key agreement. By year end, that figure was approximately 13%. [Benchmark] That is a 6× increase in under 12 months. [Pause] The trigger was a single browser update: Google Chrome 124, released April 17, 2024, enabling post-quantum key agreement by default. Firefox is following; Apple Safari has begun testing.

HTTP/3 reached 21% of global traffic — meaningful penetration for a protocol that delivers faster connections and built-in encryption. Go surpassed Node.js to become the top API client language at roughly 12% of automated requests.

[Scan Room] The strategic implication is clear: browser defaults are the fastest enterprise encryption policy lever that exists. Organizations that have not planned post-quantum migration should begin immediately — adoption is accelerating without waiting for them.

Key points: (1) PQE 2%→13%: browser defaults drive faster transitions than any enterprise mandate (2) HTTP/3 at 21% — QUIC adoption creates new infrastructure assumptions (3) Go #1 API language signals infrastructure automation stack shifts
Duration: 2.5 minutes
Flex: [If time is tight, focus on PQE slide and mention HTTP/3 and Go statistics briefly]

---

# 05_disruptions

[Transition] Now let's look at where the Internet broke down. Cloudflare tracked 225 major Internet disruptions globally in 2024.

The leading cause was not technical failure. It was not weather, cable cuts, or cyber attack. [Pause] The leading cause was government-directed shutdowns — 116 or more incidents, accounting for more than half of all disruptions observed. [Data] To put this in context: government actions caused more disruptions than cable cuts (41), power outages (16), technical problems (9), military action (9), and weather (8) *combined*.

[Benchmark] In prior years, cable cuts were the dominant physical cause. In 2024, deliberate political action overtook physical failure as the primary Internet disruption vector. This is a fundamental shift in the threat model for connectivity resilience.

[Scan Room] For organizations with operations in politically sensitive regions, this data is not just an observation — it is an infrastructure design requirement. Multi-path connectivity and regional fallback planning are now table-stakes.

Key points: (1) 225 disruptions: government shutdowns are now the #1 cause — a political, not technical, risk (2) 116+ intentional shutdowns = 51% of all disruptions (3) Cable cuts second at 41; traditional physical threats remain significant
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_security

[Transition] The disruption picture is sobering, but the security landscape confirms that even traffic that reaches its destination faces persistent threats.

Cloudflare mitigated 6.5% of all processed traffic — nearly 1 in 15 requests required active intervention. [Pause] The most attacked sector was Gambling and Games. And in a finding that should concern every security team: [Data] Log4j, a vulnerability disclosed in December 2021, is still being actively exploited more than three years later.

[Benchmark] The email threat numbers reinforce this: 4.3% of processed emails were malicious, and 43% of those contained deceptive links. The top malicious TLD was .bar — a reminder that unconventional domain extensions are now active attack vectors.

The positive signal: RPKI valid routes increased 6.4%, reflecting meaningful progress in routing security hardening. [Scan Room] But routing security progress does not offset the reality that the threat surface is broad, constant, and slow to close.

Key points: (1) 6.5% mitigation rate at Cloudflare scale = massive absolute threat volume (2) Log4j persistence = patch discipline is a long-tail obligation, not a one-time event (3) Email threats require TLD-aware, link-analysis filtering
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_takeaways

[Transition] We've covered six dimensions of 2024 Internet data. Let me close with five strategic takeaways that should directly inform your 2025 planning.

First: traffic growth is structural, not cyclical. 17% YoY with Starlink at 3.3× means your infrastructure capacity planning must assume continued acceleration.

Second: post-quantum encryption is no longer a future concern — it is a present transition. 2% to 13% in one year, driven by browser defaults. Begin migration planning now.

Third: Internet fragility is increasingly political. 116+ government shutdowns made deliberate state action the leading outage cause. Build for it.

Fourth: persistent threats demand persistent defense. Log4j is 3+ years old and still exploited. 6.5% of traffic is malicious. Assume ongoing pressure, not episodic campaigns.

Fifth: the developer ecosystem is shifting toward Go and HTTP/3. Align your API gateway, CDN, and automation investments to the protocols and languages your developers are actually using.

[Pause] The Internet in 2024 grew faster, encrypted more aggressively, fragmented politically, and remained under constant attack. 2025 planning must account for all four dimensions simultaneously.

Key points: (1) Five findings span infrastructure, encryption, geopolitics, security, and developer tooling (2) Each has a specific 2025 action item — not just observation (3) The convergence of these trends demands integrated strategy, not point solutions
Duration: 2 minutes

Global Internet traffic grew 17% year-over-year. [Data] That is nearly one-fifth more traffic than 2023 — driven by commerce, communications, entertainment, and an expanding user base. [Pause]

The headline surprise is Starlink. [Data] SpaceX Starlink traffic grew 3.3 times — meaning the satellite network delivered more than triple the traffic volume versus the prior year. [Benchmark] This growth rate dwarfs the global 17% average by nearly 20x, reflecting genuine infrastructure buildout into previously unserved regions.

[Scan Room] The 41% mobile share and 28% IPv6 adoption complement this picture — connectivity is diversifying in both medium and protocol.

Key points: (1) 17% YoY traffic growth continues multi-year upward trend (2) Starlink 3.3× signals satellite as serious infrastructure tier (3) Mobile and IPv6 adoption reflect infrastructure diversification
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_top10_services

[Transition] With more traffic on the network, the question becomes: where is that traffic going? The top 10 services ranking tells us.

Google held the #1 position for the second consecutive year, followed by Facebook, Apple, TikTok, and AWS. [Pause] The top five represent search, social, hardware, short-form video, and cloud infrastructure — a snapshot of where digital attention concentrates.

The most strategically significant trend, however, is not in the table. [Data] Generative AI services continued their rapid ascent throughout 2024, while Metaverse-associated services retreated. [Benchmark] The shift from Metaverse to Generative AI represents a complete inversion of enterprise technology investment narratives from just two years ago.

[Scan Room] For network planning purposes, the continued dominance of Google, Meta properties, and AWS means your peering and caching strategies for these platforms remain highest-priority.

Key points: (1) Google #1 for 2nd year, stable top-5 composition (2) Generative AI fastest-rising category — strategic investment signal (3) Metaverse decline confirms AI as dominant enterprise tech vector
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 04_tech_adoption

[Transition] Beyond where traffic goes, we also saw dramatic shifts in *how* it travels and *how* it is protected.

The most significant story is post-quantum encryption. [Data] At the start of 2024, approximately 2% of TLS 1.3 traffic used post-quantum key agreement. By year end, that figure was approximately 13%. [Benchmark] That is a 6× increase in under 12 months. [Pause] The trigger was a single browser update: Google Chrome 124, released April 17, 2024, enabling post-quantum key agreement by default. Firefox is following; Apple Safari has begun testing.

HTTP/3 reached 21% of global traffic — meaningful penetration for a protocol that delivers faster connections and built-in encryption. Go surpassed Node.js to become the top API client language at roughly 12% of automated requests.

[Scan Room] The strategic implication is clear: browser defaults are the fastest enterprise encryption policy lever that exists. Organizations that have not planned post-quantum migration should begin immediately — adoption is accelerating without waiting for them.

Key points: (1) PQE 2%→13%: browser defaults drive faster transitions than any enterprise mandate (2) HTTP/3 at 21% — QUIC adoption creates new infrastructure assumptions (3) Go #1 API language signals infrastructure automation stack shifts
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 05_disruptions

[Transition] Now let's look at where the Internet broke down. Cloudflare tracked 225 major Internet disruptions globally in 2024.

The leading cause was not technical failure. It was not weather, cable cuts, or cyber attack. [Pause] The leading cause was government-directed shutdowns — 116 or more incidents, accounting for more than half of all disruptions observed. [Data] To put this in context: government actions caused more disruptions than cable cuts (41), power outages (16), technical problems (9), military action (9), and weather (8) *combined*.

[Benchmark] In prior years, cable cuts were the dominant physical cause. In 2024, deliberate political action overtook physical failure as the primary Internet disruption vector. This is a fundamental shift in the threat model for connectivity resilience.

[Scan Room] For organizations with operations in politically sensitive regions, this data is not just an observation — it is an infrastructure design requirement. Multi-path connectivity and regional fallback planning are now table-stakes.

Key points: (1) 225 disruptions: government shutdowns are now the #1 cause — a political, not technical, risk (2) 116+ intentional shutdowns = 51% of all disruptions (3) Cable cuts second at 41; traditional physical threats remain significant
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_security

[Transition] The disruption picture is sobering, but the security landscape confirms that even traffic that reaches its destination faces persistent threats.

Cloudflare mitigated 6.5% of all processed traffic — nearly 1 in 15 requests required active intervention. [Pause] The most attacked sector was Gambling and Games. And in a finding that should concern every security team: [Data] Log4j, a vulnerability disclosed in December 2021, is still being actively exploited more than three years later.

[Benchmark] The email threat numbers reinforce this: 4.3% of processed emails were malicious, and 43% of those contained deceptive links. The top malicious TLD was .bar — a reminder that unconventional domain extensions are now active attack vectors.

The positive signal: RPKI valid routes increased 6.4%, reflecting meaningful progress in routing security hardening. [Scan Room] But routing security progress does not offset the reality that the threat surface is broad, constant, and slow to close.

Key points: (1) 6.5% mitigation rate at Cloudflare scale = massive absolute threat volume (2) Log4j persistence = patch discipline is a long-tail obligation, not a one-time event (3) Email threats require TLD-aware, link-analysis filtering
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 07_takeaways

[Transition] We've covered six dimensions of 2024 Internet data. Let me close with five strategic takeaways that should directly inform your 2025 planning.

First: traffic growth is structural, not cyclical. 17% YoY with Starlink at 3.3× means your infrastructure capacity planning must assume continued acceleration.

Second: post-quantum encryption is no longer a future concern — it is a present transition. 2% to 13% in one year, driven by browser defaults. Begin migration planning now.

Third: Internet fragility is increasingly political. 116+ government shutdowns made deliberate state action the leading outage cause. Build for it.

Fourth: persistent threats demand persistent defense. Log4j is 3+ years old and still exploited. 6.5% of traffic is malicious. Assume ongoing pressure, not episodic campaigns.

Fifth: the developer ecosystem is shifting toward Go and HTTP/3. Align your API gateway, CDN, and automation investments to the protocols and languages your developers are actually using.

[Pause] The Internet in 2024 grew faster, encrypted more aggressively, fragmented politically, and remained under constant attack. 2025 planning must account for all four dimensions simultaneously.

Key points: (1) Five findings span infrastructure, encryption, geopolitics, security, and developer tooling (2) Each has a specific 2025 action item — not just observation (3) The convergence of these trends demands integrated strategy, not point solutions
Duration: 2 minutes
